title: Making ricotta from goat's whey
subtitle: Whey from cheesemaking still carries enough protein to make ricotta. The second curd from the same milk, soft and fresh.
excerpt: Ricotta is made by re-cooking whey left from cheesemaking. The name means 'recooked'. Goat's whey gives a cleaner, less sweet ricotta than cow's whey, and the yield, typically 200-400 g from 4 litres of whey, makes it worth doing whenever you make a hard or semi-hard cheese the same day.
sourceNotes: Carla Emery, Encyclopedia of Country Living (1994), chapter on cheesemaking and whey. USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning (public domain), general dairy science background. Public-domain European recipe references for ricotta production technique.

glossaryTerms.definition: The liquid remaining after milk has been curdled and strained in cheesemaking. Contains residual protein (albumin and globulin), lactose, and water. Whey from acid-set cheeses ricotta more easily than whey from rennet-set hard cheeses.
A heat-sensitive whey protein that denatures and rises to the surface when whey is reheated above 80°C. The basis of ricotta. Distinct from casein, which forms in cheesemaking at lower temperatures.

content.text: left from a morning's cheesemaking will make ricotta in under an hour. The second curd is softer and more delicate than the first, good spread on bread with honey or stirred into pasta with summer herbs. Use the whey the same day; whey held overnight begins to sour and the ricotta from old whey is sharper.

Whey from an acid-set cheese, such as chèvre or lemon curd, is acid enough to make ricotta on its own. Whey from a rennet-set hard cheese needs extra acid to make the albumin coagulate. Add 30 ml of white wine vinegar or lemon juice per 4 litres of whey.
Pour the whey into a large saucepan. Add any acid now.
Heat slowly over a medium heat, stirring gently once or twice. The
begins to rise to the surface at around 80°C. Watch for white flecks forming in the whey.
Do not stir once the curd begins to form. Stirring breaks the curd into very fine particles that drain through the muslin.
Bring to 90-95°C and hold for 5 minutes. The curd should have formed a surface layer of white grains or a white foam.
Remove from heat. Allow to rest undisturbed for 15 minutes.

Line a colander with muslin and ladle the curd in gently. Let it drain for 20-60 minutes depending on how firm you want the result. A short drain gives a moist, spreadable ricotta. A longer drain gives a firmer cheese that holds its shape.

From 4 litres of fresh whey expect 150-350 g of ricotta. The yield is lower from whey that has been standing and partially acidifying, and lower from rennet-set whey than from acid-set. Use the ricotta within 3 days, kept in a sealed container in the fridge.
